newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: SKorea posts record current account deficit in '96.
newsitem.headline: SKorea posts record current account deficit in '96.

text.p: South Korea posted a record current account deficit of $23.72 billion in 1996 with key export items hit hard by plunging prices, the central bank said on Sunday.
"Falling international prices for the nation's major exports were largely to blame for the 1996 deficit," said Kim Young-bae, assistant director of the Bank of Korea's statistics division.
With exports stagnant, bank officials said the country's gross domestic product was estimated to have grown by a real 6.9 percent in 1996, down from 9.0 percent in 1995.
The $23.72 billion deficit in the current account, which covers trade in goods and services as well as transfers, compared with a shortfall of $8.95 billion in 1995, it said.
South Korea's economic planners have said top priority will be placed on reducing the deficit to between $14-$18 billion this year.
The bank figures showed export prices dropped 61 percent for semiconductors, 14.8 percent for chemicals and eight percent for steel products.
Kim said those items accounted for about 40 percent of South Korea's exports.
In value terms, semiconductor exports fell to $17.8 billion in 1996 from $22.1 billion in 1995 and steel products dropped to $7.3 billion from $10 billion.
A sharp rise in imports of consumer goods, crude oil and telecommunications and information-related equipment contributed to the deficit, Kim said.
Overall exports rose 4.1 percent in 1996 to $128.25 billion, compared with a 31.5 percent increase in 1995. Imports rose 12.1 percent to $143.53, against a rise of 32.1 percent the previous year.
Analysts said a slowdown in the world economy and a weak yen against the dollar contributed to a slowdown in export growth.
Imports of foods and consumer goods increased 21.2 percent in 1996, crude oil 33.5 percent and precision equipment 20.2 percent.
"Import price for crude rose 15.9 percent last year," Kim said.

Reflecting the slowing economy, imports of capital goods rose 10 percent in 1996, down sharply from a 32.5 percent rise in 1995. The increase in raw material imports slowed to 10.2 percent from last year's 32.6 percent.
The central bank said the deficit in the invisible trade account more than doubled to $7.68 billion in 1996 from $3.64 billion in 1995.
"The deficit is largely due to a surge in overseas travelling by South Koreans and a rise in transportation costs," said Kim.
South Koreans' overseas travel rose 21.8 percent in 1996, the bank said.
